summary: San Diego County stretches across 4,240 square miles — larger than Rhode Island and Delaware combined — and within that footprint you can drive from sea-level surf breaks to the 6,500-foot Cuyamaca Mountains in about ninety minutes, passing through coastal bluffs, deep chaparral canyons, avocado-studded foothills, and high desert on the way. That geographic range creates wildly different daily lives under one county umbrella: dense, walkable urban corridors near the harbor and Balboa Park's 1,200 acres share jurisdiction with genuinely rural backcountry where the nearest grocery run is a thirty-minute drive. The employment base is unusually layered — major military installations, a deep biotech and pharmaceutical corridor, two large research universities, and a sizable cross-border logistics economy mean job-switchers often stay within the region. But housing absorbs that income aggressively: the median home sits at roughly $791,600 against a median household income of about $102,000, producing a price-to-income ratio near 7.7, which pushes median rent to $2,154 and makes ownership arithmetic tight even at above-median earnings. The annual climate data is almost suspiciously pleasant — averaging 74°F daytime highs with ten hours of daily sunshine year-round — yet that consistency masks a county where coastal fog and inland triple-digit heat can exist on the same afternoon. San Diego is less a single city experience than a collection of microclimates, micro-economies, and micro-commutes held together by congested freeways and an ocean view everyone shares unevenly.
